# Today's Data - NHL

![](images/hr-face-off.png){fig-alt="An image from the show Heated Rivals where Shane Hollander is facing off with Ilya Rosanov."}


## Data Context - NHL Player Statistics

The data for today is taken from [this Kaggle dataset](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/xavya77/nhl04to18) of NHL player
statistics. The data contain statistics on every NHL player for the 
2004 through 2018 seasons assembled by Xavya. 

- Data were scraped from: <https://www.hockey-reference.com/> 
- Skater statistics were scraped from: <https://www.hockey-reference.com/leagues/NHL_2018_skaters.html>
- Hart MVP voting was scraped from:
<https://www.hockey-reference.com/awards/hart.html>

## Data Context - NHL Player Birthdays

We also added in [this Tidy Tuesday dataset](https://github.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/blob/main/data/2024/2024-01-09/readme.md) of player height, weight, and birthday information.

This information was acquired through the [NHL API](https://github.com/Zmalski/NHL-API-Reference).

## Observations & Variables 

::: {.midi}
Each row is a player's statistics from one `season`. The variables measured
about each player are:

::: {.incremental}
* identification: `first_name`, `last_name`
* physicals: `height`, `weight`, `age` (for that season)
* birth Information: `birth_date`, `birth_day`, `birth_month`, `birth_city`,
`birth_country`, `birth_state_province`
* position & team: `team`, `position_code` (right wing, left wing, center, 
or defense), `position_type` (forward or defense), and `sweater_number`.
* statistics for the season: `games_played`, `goals`, `assists`, `points`
(goals plus assists), `plusminus` (team goal differential when player is
playing), and `penalty_minutes`.

:::
:::

## Posing a Question

</br>

We will use these data to try to address this question: 

> What features of an NHL player are associated with them scoring more points
> (goals + assists) in a particular season?

## Addressing Unusual Observations

Based on what you found in these visuals, there are a few extreme observations
in some of the variables. There are two possible explanations for these extreme
values:

1. These represent a player that genuinely had an extreme performance in a
season.

2. These are data entry or recording errors.

Either way, we will choose to omit them, since they might be misleading to our
results.

## R & Python Code

**R Code**

::: {.midi}
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: false

data_nhl <- data_nhl |>
  filter(
    points < 200,
    penalty_minutes < 400,
    games_played > 50
  )
```
:::

**Python Code**

::: {.midi}
```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: false

data_nhl = data_nhl[
    (data_nhl["points"] < 200) &
    (data_nhl["penalty_minutes"] < 400) &
    (data_nhl["games_played"] > 50)
]
```
:::

## Addressing Unusual Observations

These visualizations should reveal two issues:

1. For some reason, the entries for the `2009` season are listed twice.  We will
simply delete the duplicates.

2. The `birth_city`, `birth_state_province`, and `birth_country` variables have
far too many different values to reasonable use.  

- We will use the `country` variable only, and we will limit its values to 
`"Canada"`, `"United States"`, or `"Other"`.

## R Code

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: false

data_nhl <- data_nhl |>
  distinct(season, 
           team, 
           first_name, 
           last_name, 
           .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  mutate(
    can_or_usa = fct_lump(birth_country, n = 2)
  ) 
```

## Python Code

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: false

data_nhl = data_nhl.drop_duplicates(
  subset = ["season", "team", "first_name", "last_name"]
  )

top_countries = (
  data_nhl["birth_country"]
  .value_counts()
  .nlargest(2)
  .index
)

data_nhl["can_or_usa"] = (
  data_nhl["birth_country"]
  .where(data_nhl["birth_country"].isin(top_countries),
         "Other")
  )
```

## Which of these variables are associated with scoring points?

We will answer this question with a *predictive model*. 

- Information from **predictor variables** will help us guess the value of 
the **target variable** (`points`).

</br>

To decide which variable(s) to use as *predictors*, we need to find the 
variables with the **strongest** relationship with `points`.

## Multiple Variables

Sometimes, the way one variable associates with `points` might be different
depending on another variables. 

For example, it is believed that players who are born earlier in the month are
more likely to become professional athletes. 

But! It may be that this trend only applies in some countries, since not all
countries have the same youth sports system. Let's see!

```{r}
#| label: points-by-birth-faceted-by-country-R
#| echo: false
#| eval: false

data_nhl |>
  mutate(birth_month = as.factor(birth_month)) |> 
  ggplot(data = data_nhl, 
         mapping = aes(x = points, y = birth_month)
         ) +
  geom_density_ridges() +
  facet_wrap(~can_or_usa)
```

```{python}
)
```

## Make Predictor Recipes

Now, we are ready to prepare our **recipes**: the different combinations of
predictors that we think could produce a good model.

We'll try two recipes today:

* One with *all* the possible predictors

* One with only the three "best" predictors that you choose.

## R & Python Code

**R Code**

::: {.midi}
```{r}
#| label: recipes-R
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: false

library(tidymodels)

rec_all <- recipe(points ~ height + weight + age + can_or_usa + 
                  birth_month + position_code + season + team + 
                  penalty_minutes, data = data_nhl)

rec_best <- recipe(points ~ position_type + season + team, 
                   data = data_nhl)
```
:::

**Python Code**

::: {.midi}
```{python}
#| echo: true
#| label: specify-variables-python
#| code-line-numbers: false

vars_all = ["height", "weight", "age", "can_or_usa", "birth_month", 
            "position_code", "season", "team", "penalty_minutes"]

vars_best = ["position_type", "season", "team"]
```
:::

## Specifying Candidate Models

::: {.midi}
The other decision we must make  is which *model types* to try.

In this analysis, we will try *Linear Regression* and a *Decision Tree*. 

- Linear regression is a natural choice since we have a continuous numerical
outcome and the interpretations are quite simple. 

- A decision tree is a simple choice for a non-statistical model that also has
easy interpretations. 


::: {.callout-warning}
There are many, many, many different model types that we can use for any given
modeling problem.

There is no magic formula for deciding which ones to try.  As you get more
experience with modeling, you'll develop more instincts for what range of
options to try.
:::
:::

## R & Python Code

**R Code**

::: {.midi}
```{r}
#| code-line-numbers: false
#| echo: true

lr_spec <- linear_reg() |>
  set_mode("regression")

dt_spec <- decision_tree(min_n = 10) |>
  set_mode("regression") 
```
:::

**Python Code**

::: {.midi}
```{python}
#| code-line-numbers: false
#| echo: true

from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor

lr_spec = LinearRegression()

dt_spec = DecisionTreeRegressor(min_samples_leaf = 10)
```

<!-- ::: {.callout-important} -->
<!-- A decision tree has a **hyperparameter** we can specify---`min_samples_leaf` or -->
<!-- `min_n`. This parameter represents the smallest number of observations that a -->
<!-- leaf (a part of the tree) is allowed to have. -->
<!-- ::: -->
:::

## Pre-Processing Options

Recall that we noticed a few interesting things in our exploratory data
analysis:

* `penalty_minutes` is very right-skewed 

* Birth country seems to impact how birth month impacts the target. 

We will add a *transformation* and an *interaction* to our workflow.

## R & Python Code

</br>

::: columns
::: {.column width="48%"}
### R Code

Specify transformer **and** variable(s) **at the same time**

```{r}
#| label: create-recipes-for-variable-transformation

rec_all <- rec_all |>
  step_log(penalty_minutes) |>
  step_dummy(can_or_usa, position_code) |>
  step_interact(~ birth_month*contains("can_or_usa"))

rec_best <- rec_best |>
  step_log(penalty_minutes) |>
  step_dummy(can_or_usa, position_code) |>
  step_interact( ~ birth_month*contains("can_or_usa"))
```

:::

::: {.column width="4%"}
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
### Python Code

Specify "general" transformer, then apply the transformer to specific columns.

<div class="tenor-gif-embed" data-postid="12103154902932132925" data-share-method="host" data-aspect-ratio="1.33125" data-width="70%"><a href="https://tenor.com/view/hudconfansdr-gif-12103154902932132925">Hudconfansdr GIF</a>from <a href="https://tenor.com/search/hudconfansdr-gifs">Hudconfansdr GIFs</a></div> <script type="text/javascript" async src="https://tenor.com/embed.js"></script>

```{python}
#| label: make-general-transformers

import numpy as np
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, FunctionTransformer, PolynomialFeatures

categorical_transformer = Pipeline([
    ("onehot", OneHotEncoder(drop="first", handle_unknown="ignore"))
])

log_transformer = Pipeline([
    ("log", FunctionTransformer(np.log1p, validate = True))
])

interact_transformer = Pipeline([
  ("onehot", OneHotEncoder(drop = "first")),
  ("interact", PolynomialFeatures(interaction_only=True, include_bias=False))
])
```

```{python}
#| label: use-transformers-on-specific-columns

from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer

rec_all = ColumnTransformer([
    ("cat", categorical_transformer, ["position_code", "season", "team"]),
    ("int", interact_transformer, ["can_or_usa", "birth_month"]),
    ("log", log_transformer, ["penalty_minutes"]),
    ("num", "passthrough", ["age", "height", "weight"])
    ],
    remainder = "drop"
)

rec_best = ColumnTransformer([
    ("cat", categorical_transformer, ["position_type", "season", "team"])],
    remainder="drop")

```

:::
:::

## Combining Data & Models

</br>

We will try all our different **model type** options with all our
different **recipe and preprocessing** choices.

Each of these candidate options is called a **workflow** or a **pipeline**.

## R & Python Code

**R Code (Template)**

::: {.midi}
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
#| code-line-numbers: false

workflow() |>
  add_model() |>
  add_recipe()
```

```{r}
#| label: specify-model-and-transformers-R

# Linear regression with all predictors
wflow_lr_all <- workflow() |>
  add_model(lr_spec) |>
  add_recipe(rec_all)

# Linear regression with best predictors
wflow_lr_best <- workflow() |>
  add_model(lr_spec) |>
  add_recipe(rec_best)

# Decision tree with all predictors
wflow_dt_all <- workflow() |>
  add_model(dt_spec) |>
  add_recipe(rec_all)

# Decision tree with best predictors
wflow_dt_best <- workflow() |>
  add_model(dt_spec) |>
  add_recipe(rec_best)

```
:::

</br>

**Python Code (Template)**

::: {.midi}
```{python}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
#| code-line-numbers: false

from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.base import clone

make_pipeline(clone(recipe), clone(model))

```

```{python}
#| label: specify-model-and-transformers-python

from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.base import clone

# Linear regression with all predictors
wflow_lr_all = make_pipeline(clone(rec_all), clone(lr_spec))

# Linear regression with best predictors
wflow_lr_best = make_pipeline(clone(rec_best), clone(lr_spec))

# Decision tree with all predictors
wflow_dt_all = make_pipeline(clone(rec_all), clone(dt_spec))

# Decision tree with best predictors
wflow_dt_best = make_pipeline(clone(rec_best), clone(dt_spec))

```
:::

# Step 4 -- Choosing between Competing Models

Everything we have done to this point was *setup*.🤪 But now we're ready to 
try out our workflows!

## Comparing Models

::: {.midi}
Now, how will we compare the four options and see which one is most successful
at predicting `points`?  
:::

. . .

::: {.midi}
The process goes like this:

1. Randomly set aside 20% of our data rows as a *test set*.  The rest is called
the *training set*.

2. Fit all of the workflows on the *training set*.

3. See how well each fitted workflow does at predicting on the *test set*.
:::

. . .

::: {.small}
:::{.callout-warning}
In Part 2 of the workshop, you will learn about using **cross-validation** to
choose between different models. This is essentially the process of creating
*many different* test/training splits.
:::
:::

## Test / Train Split

**R Code**

::: {.midi}
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: false
#| label: test-train-split-R

set.seed(2244)

split <- initial_split(data_nhl, prop = 0.8)

data_nhl_train <- training(split)
data_nhl_test <- testing(split)
```
:::

**Python Code**

::: {.midi}
```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: false
#| label: test-train-split-python

from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split


data_nhl_train, data_nhl_test = train_test_split(data_nhl, 
                                                 test_size = 0.2, 
                                                 random_state = 2244)
```
:::

## Fit Our Models on the Training Data

**R Code (Template)**

::: {.midi}
```{r}
#| label: fit-models-to-training-data-R
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: false

# Fit workflow on training data
wflow_lr_all_fit <- fit(wflow_lr_all, 
                        data = data_nhl_train)
```
:::

</br>

**Python Code (Template)**

::: {.midi}
```{python}
#| label: fit-models-to-training-data-python-ex
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: false

# Split data into predictor variables
X_train = data_nhl_train.drop(columns = ["points"])
# and target variable
y_train = data_nhl_train["points"]

# Fit workflow on training data
wflow_lr_all_fit = wflow_lr_all.fit(X_train, y_train)
```

```{python}
#| label: fit-models-to-training-data-python-rest

wflow_lr_best_fit = wflow_lr_best.fit(X_train, y_train)
wflow_dt_all_fit = wflow_dt_all.fit(X_train, y_train)
wflow_dt_best_fit = wflow_dt_best.fit(X_train, y_train)
```
:::

## Assess Models on Test Data

Finally, we will use these fitted models to make predictions on the test data, 
and we'll see how close these predictions were to the true observed values for
`points`

::: {.midi}
:::{.callout-note}
In this analysis, we are using *root mean squared error* as our **metric** for
the test data.  That is, we take the squared difference between the *predicted* 
number of points a player will get and the *actual* number of points they get, 
then we add those numbers up and take the average. 

</br>

$$ \sqrt \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}{n}$$
:::
:::

```{python}
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error

# Separate features and outcome from test set
X_test = data_nhl_test.drop(columns = ["points"])
y_test = data_nhl_test["points"]

# Make predictions
pred_lr_all = wflow_lr_all_fit.predict(X_test)
pred_lr_best = wflow_lr_best_fit.predict(X_test)
pred_dt_all = wflow_dt_all_fit.predict(X_test)
pred_dt_best = wflow_dt_best_fit.predict(X_test)

# Calculate prediction errors
rmse_lr_all = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_test, pred_lr_all))
rmse_lr_best = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_test, pred_lr_best))
rmse_dt_all = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_test, pred_dt_all))
rmse_dt_best = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_test, pred_dt_best))

print("RMSE (Linear All):", rmse_lr_all)
print("RMSE (Linear Best):", rmse_lr_best)
print("RMSE (Tree All):", rmse_dt_all)
print("RMSE (Tree Best):", rmse_dt_best)

```

## Interpreting your Final Model

- Sometimes, the goal of your machine learning process is simply to **produce a 
model**. 
    * You can use the model to predict which players you should draft!

. . .

- Other times, the goal is more about **interpretation**. 
    * You want to tell stories about the patterns in the data.

. . .

Since our best final model was a *decision tree*, we'll make a 
**dendrogram** visualizing the splits. 

## In R

```{r}
#| label: final-model-R
#| echo: false

final_model <- fit(wflow_dt_all, data = data_nhl)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| eval: false

# Declare predictor variables
X_full = data_nhl.drop(columns = ["points"])
# Declare target variable
y_full = data_nhl["points"]

final_model = wflow_dt_all.fit(X_full, y_full)
```


```{r}
#| label: dendrogram-plot-R
#| echo: true
#| eval: true
#| code-line-numbers: false

library(rpart.plot)

# Pull out the parsnip model object
tree_fit <- extract_fit_parsnip(final_model)

rpart.plot(tree_fit$fit, roundint = FALSE)
```

## In Python

```{python}
#| label: dendrogram-plot-python
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
#| code-line-numbers: false

from sklearn.tree import plot_tree
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

n_features = final_model.named_steps["decisiontreeregressor"].n_features_in_
feature_names = [f"feature_{i}" for i in range(n_features)]

plt.figure(figsize=(16, 8))
plot_tree(
    final_model.named_steps["decisiontreeregressor"],
    feature_names=feature_names,
    filled=True,
    rounded=True,
    max_depth=3
)
plt.show()

```

# Step 6 -- Ethical Considerations

<div class="tenor-gif-embed" data-postid="11102954406056326040" data-share-method="host" data-aspect-ratio="1" data-width="50%"><a href="https://tenor.com/view/kip-grady-heated-rivalry-gif-11102954406056326040">Kip Grady Heated Rivalry GIF</a>from <a href="https://tenor.com/search/kip+grady-gifs">Kip Grady GIFs</a></div> <script type="text/javascript" async src="https://tenor.com/embed.js"></script>

## Models that can do harm

::: {.midi}
- Predictive models are great at **predicting**. 
- Predictive models are not great in knowing if their model is **harmful**. 
:::

. . .

::: {.midi}
Suppose instead we wanted to predict a student's likelihood of success in
college. Our predictive model suggests that: 

::: columns
::: {.column width="48%"}
- `zip_code`, 
- `parental_education`, 
:::

::: {.column width="4%"}
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
- `first_generation`
- `standardized_exam_score` 
:::
:::

are strongly related to students' college performance. 
:::

. . .

</br>

::: {style="font-size: 1.25em; color: #ed8402;"}
**Who does this model privilege? Who is being harmed by this model?**
:::

<!-- Socioeconomic Status Proxies -->
<!-- Zip code or neighborhood of residence (correlates with school quality and resources) -->
<!-- High school attended (public vs. private, school district funding) -->
<!-- Parental education level and occupation -->
<!-- Extracurricular activities (cost money, require parental transportation, free time) -->
<!-- Unpaid internship or volunteer experience (requires financial cushion) -->

<!-- Race-Correlated Variables -->
<!-- "First-generation college student" status (disproportionately students of color) -->
<!-- High school GPA from under-resourced schools (grading environments differ) -->
<!-- Standardized test scores (well-documented score gaps driven largely by resource access, not ability) -->
